hypothesis: The neuron responds selectively to localized, high-contrast communicative or symbolic markings, specifically text strings, logos, signage, and geometric icons (e.g., arrows, play buttons), as well as structural mimics such as rows of teeth or sharp plumage stripes. The core visual driver is a horizontal arrangement of distinct, high-frequency stroke-like shapes—typically bright white, silver, or black—set against a solid, contrasting background of deep red, black, dark grey, or wood tone. The activating feature usually presents as a bounded entity (e.g., a license plate, digital display, brand label, or mouth) occupying approximately 20–50% of the frame and positioned centrally. The neuron remains invariant to the semantic content (words vs. patterns) and object material (metal, plastic, biological), provided the strong light-dark contrast and linear, organized form are preserved.
